Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Woody Allen's lawsuit against American Apparel for unauthorized use of his image on billboards ended Monday with a $5 million settlement to be paid to the actor-director by the clothing company. Woody Allen received $5 million to settle a suit with American Apparel. Allen said the case should discourage advertisers from using celebrities' images without permission, but American Apparel's head said he still thinks his company had a good defense. The settlement, announced just moments before jury selection was to begin in New York, interrupted a trial that lawyers had hinted could include a parade of witnesses testifying about Allen's sex scandals. "Threats and press leaks by American Apparel designed to smear me did not work, and a scheme to call a long list of witnesses who had nothing to do with the case was disallowed by the court," Allen said. "I hope this very large settlement will discourage American Apparel and others from doing this type of thing to myself or others in the future." Dov Charney, founder and CEO of American Apparel, issued a statement published by London's Guardian newspaper saying lawyers for his insurance company -- which will pay the money to Allen -- made the decision to settle the case. "For the record, I personally think we had a good case," Charney said. Allen filed his suit, asking for $10 million, against American Apparel in March 2008 after the company placed several billboards and online ads using an image of Allen dressed as a Hasidic Jew in his 1977 movie "Annie Hall." "I sued American Apparel because they calculatingly took my name, my likeness and image and used them publicly to promote their business," Allen said Monday. "Testimony revealed that American Apparel believed that fear of publicity would keep me from ever taking action, and so they put my face on billboards, on the Internet, and my image on their building," he said. Charney, who said he finally could talk about the case, said the ad was a "an attempt to at least make a joke about" sexual harassment lawsuits filed against him and his company in recent years. "Today, two years later, all the claims in the lawsuits have been completely disproven and yet at the time, some writers characterized me as a rapist and abuser of women, others asserted that I was a bad Jew, and some even stated that I was not fit to run my company." Charney said it was "ironic that I have to explain this to Woody Allen when he has expressed similar frustrations in the past." American Apparel lawyers wanted to call as witnesses Allen's former companion Mia Farrow and Soon-Yi Previn, Farrow's adopted daughter and Allen's wife. Allen's relationship with -- and eventual marriage to -- Previn was scandal material for tabloids beginning in 1992, when she was 21. Allen said the company's lawyers may have been persuaded to settle because the judge made it "clear that the court considered their phony First Amendment ranting and claims of parody, sheer nonsense."

## Woody Allen’s Lawsuit Against American Apparel Ends in $5 Million Settlement Before Trial

**NEW YORK —** Woody Allen’s high-profile lawsuit against American Apparel ended before a jury was ever seated, with the clothing company agreeing in May 2009 to pay the filmmaker **$5 million** over billboards and internet ads that used his image without permission.

The settlement brought an abrupt end to a case that had been expected to turn into a public airing of some of the most painful and sensational chapters of Allen’s private life, including his breakup with Mia Farrow and his relationship with Soon-Yi Previn.

### Why Allen sued American Apparel

Allen filed suit in federal court in Manhattan after American Apparel used a still image of him from his 1977 film **“Annie Hall.”** In the image, Allen appears dressed as a Hasidic Jew, a scene from the film in which his character imagines himself through the eyes of his girlfriend’s family.

The image appeared on American Apparel billboards and online advertising, accompanied by Yiddish text. Allen said the company had used his likeness without permission and falsely implied that he endorsed the brand.

The director, who has long avoided commercial endorsements in the United States, sought **$10 million** in damages. His complaint argued that the unauthorized use of his image was especially harmful because American Apparel’s advertising and public image were sexually provocative and controversial, making any implied association damaging to his reputation.

Allen’s legal position was straightforward: the company had taken his image, used it in advertising, and never obtained consent.

### American Apparel’s defense and Charney’s comments

American Apparel and its founder, **Dov Charney**, did not initially treat the billboard as a conventional celebrity endorsement. Charney said the ad was intended as a form of commentary rather than a commercial pitch.

He described the billboard as a **parody or social statement**, not an attempt to suggest that Allen wore or endorsed American Apparel clothing. The company argued that the ad was protected expression and that it was not directly selling a product in the way a typical advertisement would.

Charney also said the use of Allen’s image was tied to American Apparel’s own controversies and to broader issues of public morality, reputation and hypocrisy. In effect, the company suggested that the ad was meant to provoke discussion rather than exploit Allen’s celebrity for sales.

But that defense faced a major obstacle: the image appeared in American Apparel advertising space and was connected to the company’s branding. Allen’s lawyers argued that whatever Charney’s claimed intent, the public use of Allen’s likeness in a corporate ad campaign required permission.

### Why the case ended before trial

The case was scheduled for trial in federal court, but the two sides settled before opening arguments. American Apparel agreed to pay Allen **$5 million**, half of what he had sought.

Allen said after the settlement that the company’s use of his image was “sleazy” and that he hoped the outcome would discourage advertisers from using celebrities’ likenesses without approval. The settlement allowed him to avoid a trial that was expected to delve deeply into his personal history.

For American Apparel, the payment ended a lawsuit that had become increasingly risky. A trial could have resulted in a substantial damages award, and the company would have had to convince jurors that a billboard using a famous actor’s recognizable image was not an unauthorized commercial endorsement.

### How Mia Farrow and Soon-Yi Previn were connected to the case

Although the lawsuit was about advertising rights, it threatened to become entangled with Allen’s personal life because American Apparel’s lawyers wanted to challenge the value of his reputation.

The company signaled that it might call **Mia Farrow**, Allen’s former partner, and **Soon-Yi Previn**, Farrow’s adopted daughter who later became Allen’s wife, as witnesses or bring up issues connected to them.

Their connection to the case stemmed from Allen’s claim that the ad damaged his image and commercial value. American Apparel’s strategy was to argue that Allen’s reputation had already been affected by the public scandal surrounding his relationship with Soon-Yi and his bitter split from Farrow. By raising those events, the company hoped to reduce or undermine Allen’s damages claim.

That possibility gave the case a tabloid dimension. A trial could have revisited the early-1990s scandal in which Allen’s relationship with Soon-Yi became public while he was still linked to Farrow. It also could have revived discussion of the broader family conflict that followed.

Allen’s side sought to keep the case focused on the unauthorized use of his image. The settlement avoided the spectacle of testimony or courtroom arguments involving Farrow, Soon-Yi and the personal controversies that American Apparel appeared prepared to raise.

### A celebrity-rights case with tabloid stakes

In the end, the case never produced a definitive trial ruling on American Apparel’s parody or free-expression arguments. Instead, it ended as a costly settlement and a warning to advertisers: using a celebrity’s likeness, even in a supposedly ironic or provocative campaign, can carry serious legal consequences.

For Allen, the settlement vindicated his claim that American Apparel had no right to place him in its advertising. For Charney and the company, it closed a case that had begun with a provocative billboard but was on the verge of becoming a courtroom examination of celebrity, scandal, reputation and the commercial value of a famous face.
